texto:
Autocrediting is the process by which Google automatically refunds advertisers in Local Services Ads for leads its systems later judge to be invalid or of low quality. Local Services Ads charge per lead, typically a phone call, message or booking, rather than per click. A charge that turns out to be a wrong number, a spam call or a duplicate is money spent on nothing. Autocrediting exists to return that money without the advertiser having to ask. The word appears in Google's own help documentation, which describes credited leads as charges reversed "either through autocrediting or as a bonus credit for leaving feedback". It replaced a manual dispute process that Google retired from July 2024.
The term has no standard definition outside Google. Other automatic refunds in advertising, such as invalid click credits in Google Ads, are usually called credits or adjustments instead. This explainer concerns the Local Services Ads meaning, which is the only one where the single word is in established use.
How a lead is screened and credited
The mechanism has two stages. According to Google's help page on automated lead credits, machine learning models assess each lead "when a potential customer first makes contact". A lead judged invalid or low quality at that point is never charged. That is screening, not crediting.
The second stage is autocrediting proper. Leads that were charged are reassessed over time, and those "later determined to be low quality" may be credited automatically. Google concedes that the first stage is imperfect: some poor leads "processed via auto credits" can still appear within the first 24 hours. Credits are applied to the account balance "in most cases" within 30 days. The original charge stays on the invoice, with the credit shown separately.
The leads report sorts every lead into one of four statuses:
- Not charged: never billed, for reasons such as low quality or duplication.
- Charged: billed from the start and not reversed.
- In review: under evaluation, with a credit applied if the lead "isn't a good match".
- Credited: billed and then refunded, by autocrediting or as a feedback bonus.
The same states are exposed to software. In the Google Ads API, the LocalServicesLead resource carries a lead_charged field and a credit_details object, whose credit_state takes the values CREDITED or PENDING, along with a timestamp of the last change in the account's time zone.
Which leads qualify matters as much as how they are found. According to a July 2024 guide from the agency Camp Digital, the reasons that still lead to a credit are wrong numbers or sales calls, spam or bot contacts, duplicate leads and calls meant for a different business. Two former reasons were dropped. Google's help page states that it no longer credits leads marked "job type not serviced" or "geo not serviced". A plumber called about roofing, or by a customer two counties outside the service area, now pays for that lead. Google suggests tightening service areas and job types instead.
Eligibility is also limited. Google says lead credits "aren't available for health care verticals, tax specialists, or advertisers in EMEA", meaning Europe, the Middle East and Africa.
On the buy side sits a local business, often a plumber, locksmith or lawyer, or its agency. On the sell side, Google sets the lead price, runs the models and issues the credit. No third party audits the decision.
From manual disputes to automated credits
Local Services Ads began as Google Home Services, a beta launched in 2015, and was renamed Local Services by Google in 2017. Search Engine Land reported at the rebrand that Google set lead prices by job type and area rather than through an auction, with advertisers choosing a weekly budget.
Pay-per-lead pricing created a need for refunds from the start. For most of the product's life, advertisers who received a bad lead had to dispute it themselves. A 2023 guide from Adventure Media describes the routine: open the lead, check whether it was charged, listen to the recording or read the message, choose "Dispute Lead" and pick one of six reasons, including "service not provided" and "location not served".
Google said the system did not scale. On June 24, 2024, Ginny Marvin, Google's Ads Liaison, wrote on X that "a very small number of advertisers dispute a high share of their leads" while most "didn't dispute leads at all", as reported by Search Engine Roundtable. "Rather than waiting for advertisers to initiate disputes, we're proactively evaluating every lead that comes in," she wrote, adding that the system had been in testing "for more than a year". Search Engine Land reported that the rollout would begin in July 2024, that advertisers could not opt out and that Google expected "the same or more leads on average" to be credited for most advertisers.
Feedback replaced the dispute button. Google added a Lead Feedback survey to every lead, reached through "Rate this lead" in the dashboard. It trains the models on which leads suit each business. Lead rating is a separate feature with its own role and is covered in its own explainer. In April 2025, Google Ads API version 19.1 added a ProvideLeadFeedback method and a lead_feedback_submitted field, so ratings could be sent in bulk from a customer relationship management system.
The scope then narrowed. In January 2025, Google removed autocrediting, message leads, bookings and call recording for tax specialists, leaving that vertical without native tools to check charges.
Why the mechanism matters to advertisers
For a small business, the credit is part of the price. A lead cost is only meaningful net of the leads later refunded. One advertiser on X claimed junk legal leads cost $600 per call, a figure Google did not confirm.
The design also shifts who decides. Under disputes, an advertiser who listened to every call recovered more than one who did not; autocrediting treats all advertisers alike, which Google argued was fairer. The trade-off is that the decision now sits inside a model the advertiser cannot inspect or appeal.
Autocrediting also interacts with Google's broader move towards automated lead qualification. In April 2026 Google Ads began using AI to qualify phone call conversions from recordings rather than call length. One system decides whether a call counts as a conversion; the other, whether a charged lead is refunded.
Criticism and open questions
Complaints about lead quality followed within months. On February 11, 2025, Search Engine Roundtable reported that Darren Shaw, founder of the local search firm Whitespark, said agencies managing Local Services Ads "for hundreds of businesses" reported that "lead quality has declined significantly in the past few months". Search Engine Roundtable later noted that Shaw did not necessarily blame autocrediting. Marvin replied: "we actually credit more leads overall now than we did when advertisers had to manually dispute leads". She added that manual disputes had been "underutilized by the majority of advertisers and overused by a few".
Agencies have been more direct. Drew Hansen of PaperStreet called the end of credits for wrong-service and wrong-location calls a "major con" and Google's claim to credit more leads "very suspect". Writing for Advertising Week in June 2026, Julian Diep of Blue Grid Media argued that the platform now "quietly decides who is allowed to disagree with the outcome, and how loudly".
Several facts remain unpublished. Google has not disclosed the share of leads credited, the error rate of its models or how credits interact with ranking. Sources also disagree on details. Google's help page says feedback can earn a "bonus credit", while Camp Digital wrote in 2024 that ratings carried no direct credit. Google gives 30 days for credits; some agencies cite 72 hours for clearly invalid leads. PPC Land's January 2025 report described autocrediting as available only in the United States and Canada, while Google's help page lists exclusions by vertical and region instead.
Not the same as
- Invalid activity credits in Google Ads. Search and Performance Max campaigns are billed per click, and Google filters invalid clicks before invoicing. Clicks found invalid after the invoice closes generate credits, which Google documented in an Invalid Activity Credit Report in June 2026. These concern fraudulent or accidental clicks, not unsuitable customers.
- Overdelivery credits. According to Google Ads Help, an account receives a credit when costs exceed the average daily budget limit. This is a budget rule, not a quality judgement.
- Attribution credit. Models such as data-driven attribution assign "credit" for a conversion across ad interactions. No money changes hands.
- Automatic payment deductions. Amazon's move to deduct ad costs from seller proceeds from April 15, 2026, is a payment method, not a refund.
Recent developments
In July 2026 Google said it would fold Local Services Ads into Google Ads as Performance Max campaigns with pay-per-lead goals, starting in August 2026 with selected US home and storefront service advertisers, followed by a second phase in late 2026 and non-US accounts in 2027. Migrated advertisers lose access to the old dashboard on transition day. The new leads table in Google Ads shows a "charged" status and a feedback form, but Google's transition page, as of October 2026, does not mention lead credits.
Charging rules are widening at the same time. From October 1, 2026, Google bills missed business-hours calls where the caller stays on the line for more than 20 seconds. PPC Land's follow-up found no published dispute process or appeal route for the new charge, leaving automated reassessment as the only refund mechanism advertisers can rely on.
Timeline
- 2015: Google launches Home Services ads in beta with lead-based pricing
- 2017: Program renamed Local Services by Google
- October 19, 2023: Agency guides still describe the manual "Dispute Lead" process
- June 24, 2024: Ginny Marvin announces automated lead credits on X
- July 2024: Automated credits begin rolling out; manual disputes retired; "job type not serviced" and "geo not serviced" credits dropped
- September 2024: Target Cost Per Lead bidding launches in Local Services Ads
- January 6, 2025: Google removes autocrediting for tax specialists
- February 11, 2025: Advertisers report lead-quality decline; Google says more leads are credited than under disputes
- April 16, 2025: Google Ads API v19.1 adds ProvideLeadFeedback
- April 21, 2026: Google Ads documents AI-qualified call conversions
- June 1, 2026: Google documents the Invalid Activity Credit Report for Search and Performance Max
- July 2026: Google announces migration of Local Services Ads into Performance Max
- August 2026: First US accounts migrate
- October 1, 2026: Missed calls over 20 seconds become chargeable

Summary
Who: Google operates autocrediting for Local Services Ads advertisers, mainly local service businesses and the agencies that manage them. Health care, tax specialists and EMEA advertisers are excluded.
What: The automatic refund of charged leads that Google's machine learning models later judge invalid or low quality, such as spam, wrong numbers and duplicates, without a manual dispute.
When: Announced June 24, 2024 and rolled out from July 2024, replacing manual disputes. Removed for tax specialists in January 2025. Its place in the Performance Max migration that began in August 2026 has not been documented.
Where: Local Services Ads on Google Search and Maps, with credit states visible in the dashboard and the Google Ads API.
Why: Google said manual disputes were used heavily by a few advertisers and ignored by most, and that automated review would credit as many or more leads on average.
